faqs.a: That's common once a unit sees infill drilling, and it usually strengthens the picture rather than complicating it, since each well's statement history gives us more data to work from when estimating the unit's remaining productive life and building an offer that reflects the full position.

faqs.q: Can you sell only part of your royalty interest?
faqs.a: In many cases, yes. Some owners prefer to sell a portion of their royalty while retaining the rest, which can make sense if you want partial liquidity now while keeping some ongoing income. Ask us to walk through what a partial sale would look like for your specific interest.

items.name: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI)
items.meta: An NPRI pays a share of production but carries no leasing authority. Here's how non-participating royalty interests work for Utah owners and what they're worth.

sections.html:
A non-participating royalty interest is the cleanest, most passive form of mineral ownership: you receive a share of production, and you have no say whatsoever in leasing decisions.

An NPRI is created when a mineral owner carves out and conveys a royalty share, either to a family member, an investor, or as part of an estate settlement, while keeping (or transferring to someone else) the executive right to lease the underlying minerals. The word 'non-participating' refers specifically to leasing: the NPRI owner doesn't participate in negotiating bonus payments, setting lease terms, or deciding which operator gets to drill. What they do get is a fixed fractional share of production once a well is drilled, regardless of who negotiated the lease or what the bonus was.

We see NPRIs across Utah most often as the result of a prior generation splitting an estate: one heir received the executive rights and the working relationship with the operator, while another received a pure royalty share with none of the leasing responsibility. Both are legitimate, separately valuable interests, but they behave differently and, importantly, need to be identified correctly before either one is priced.

sections.title: What an NPRI owner does and doesn't control
sections.html:
Because an NPRI carries no executive right, the owner has no ability to negotiate a better bonus, insist on a higher royalty rate in a future lease, or refuse to allow leasing altogether. Whatever the mineral owner who holds the executive right negotiates, the NPRI owner receives their fixed fractional share of production under those terms. This makes an NPRI genuinely passive — there's no decision-making burden — but it also means the income depends entirely on someone else's leasing judgment.

This distinction matters most when a lease is up for renewal or renegotiation. An NPRI owner watching a lease term run down has no direct lever to pull; they're dependent on the executive rights holder to act. That's worth understanding clearly if you hold an NPRI and are trying to gauge how much control you actually have over your own income stream.

sections.title: How NPRI value is typically calculated
sections.html:
Valuing an NPRI starts with the fractional royalty rate specified in the conveyance that created it, applied against actual or projected production on the unit. Because the NPRI owner bears none of the drilling or operating costs, the royalty percentage translates fairly directly into income once production begins, which makes NPRIs comparatively straightforward to price once production history exists.

Where it gets more complicated is confirming exactly what fraction was conveyed and against what base — some older Utah NPRI deeds are written ambiguously enough that a title examiner needs to work through the specific language to confirm whether the fraction applies to a fixed royalty amount or floats with whatever royalty the mineral owner later negotiates. That distinction can meaningfully change the value, so we always confirm it before pricing an offer.

sections.title: Selling an NPRI
sections.html:
NPRIs are freely transferable, same as any other real property interest, and selling yours doesn't require any involvement from whoever holds the executive rights on the same minerals. If your NPRI is currently producing, we'll price it primarily off your royalty statement history and the operator's current activity; if it's tied to unleased or non-producing minerals, we'll weigh it more on proximity to activity, similar to any non-producing interest.

Because NPRIs are sometimes confused with other interest types on old paperwork, we'll confirm the conveyance language creating your interest before finalizing a number, just to make sure we're pricing what you actually own.

faqs.q: What does 'non-participating' mean in an NPRI?
faqs.a: It means the royalty owner has no say in leasing decisions — no ability to negotiate bonus payments, set lease terms, or choose the operator. They receive a fixed royalty share of production once a well is drilled, but the leasing itself is controlled by whoever holds the executive rights.

faqs.q: Can you sell your NPRI without the mineral owner's permission?
faqs.a: Yes. An NPRI is a separate, independently transferable property interest, and selling it doesn't require consent from whoever holds the executive rights to the same minerals.

faqs.q: Is an NPRI worth less than a regular mineral interest?
faqs.a: Not necessarily less valuable, just structured differently. An NPRI carries no leasing control and no executive rights, but the royalty income itself is calculated similarly to a standard royalty interest once production exists.

faqs.q: How do you know if what you have is an NPRI versus a mineral interest?
faqs.a: Check the deed or conveyance that created your interest. If it grants only a royalty share without leasing authority, it's an NPRI. If you're unsure, we can review the language with you before pricing an offer.

faqs.q: Does an NPRI survive if the current lease expires?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Because an NPRI is carved from the underlying mineral estate rather than from a specific lease, it typically survives a lease expiring and simply continues attached to the minerals, ready to receive royalty again once a new lease is signed and a well is drilled. This is a meaningful difference from an overriding royalty interest, which is tied to one lease and ends when that lease does.

faqs.q: Can an NPRI be divided among multiple heirs over time?
faqs.a: Yes, the same way any other real property interest can. An NPRI created decades ago by one family member is often fractionalized further as it passes through subsequent generations, which is worth accounting for when confirming exactly what decimal share you hold before selling.

items.name: Surface vs. Mineral Estate
items.meta: In Utah, the surface and minerals beneath it can be owned by different people entirely. Here's how split estates work and what it means for a mineral owner.

sections.html:
Two people can hold legitimate, fully recognized ownership of the exact same piece of Utah ground: one owns the surface, the other owns what's beneath it, and neither needs the other's permission to sell their own piece.

This split, formally called a severed or split estate, is one of the more confusing concepts for families who inherit mineral rights without inheriting the land those minerals sit under, or who inherit the surface without the minerals. It's also one of the most common ownership patterns in Utah, particularly in counties where homesteads and land patents from the early twentieth century reserved minerals separately, and in areas with heavy checkerboard SITLA and federal ownership woven through private surface.

Understanding which estate you own, and what rights come with it, matters because the two estates interact in specific, legally defined ways even though they're independently owned. A mineral owner generally has the right to access the surface reasonably to develop those minerals, even over a surface owner's objection, subject to compensation and reasonable-use limitations. That dynamic surprises a lot of people the first time they encounter it, on either side of the split.

sections.title: How Utah land ended up split this way
sections.html:
Much of Utah's severed mineral ownership traces back to homestead-era federal land patents, where the government reserved certain minerals when transferring surface title to homesteaders, or to later private transactions where a landowner sold the surface but kept the minerals, or vice versa. In the Uinta Basin specifically, the checkerboard pattern created by the original Uinta Reservation allotment process and subsequent land openings layered state SITLA, federal BLM, tribal trust, and private fee ownership across what looks, on a map, like a single contiguous area.

For a private mineral owner, none of that history changes your rights day to day, but it does mean your neighbor's parcel, even one that looks identical to yours on a plat map, may sit under a completely different ownership and leasing framework. That's worth confirming rather than assuming when you're trying to understand your own position.

sections.title: What each estate can and can't do
sections.html:
The mineral estate is generally considered the 'dominant' estate under longstanding oil and gas law, meaning the mineral owner (or the operator they've leased to) has an implied right to use as much of the surface as is reasonably necessary to explore for and produce minerals, including building roads, well pads, and pipelines. This right isn't unlimited — Utah law and most modern leases require reasonable accommodation of the surface owner's existing use, and surface damage compensation is standard practice — but it does mean a surface owner generally can't block reasonable mineral development outright.

A surface owner without any mineral interest has no claim to royalty income from production beneath their land and no say in leasing decisions. Conversely, a mineral owner with no surface interest has no right to build a house or graze cattle on the land above their minerals. The two estates are genuinely separate bundles of rights, each transferable and valuable on its own terms.

sections.title: What this means if you're selling
sections.html:
If you own mineral rights without the surface, that's entirely normal and fully sellable on its own — we buy mineral interests all the time from owners with no surface connection to the land whatsoever, and it doesn't complicate the transaction. What matters for pricing is the mineral estate itself: production history, lease status, and nearby activity, not who owns or uses the surface above it.

If you're unsure whether your family's interest includes the surface, the mineral estate, or both, the county recorder's chain of title will clarify it, typically through a reservation or exception clause in a deed somewhere in the history. We can help track that down as part of confirming exactly what you're able to sell.

faqs.q: Can you sell mineral rights if you don't own the surface land?
faqs.a: Yes. Mineral rights and surface rights are independently transferable once severed. Owning only the minerals doesn't limit your ability to sell that interest on its own.

faqs.q: Does the surface owner have to approve drilling on your mineral interest?
faqs.a: Generally no. The mineral estate is typically treated as the dominant estate, meaning the operator has an implied right to reasonable surface use for development, though Utah practice and most leases require reasonable accommodation and compensation for surface damage.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your minerals are severed from the surface?
faqs.a: Check the county recorder's chain of title for a mineral reservation or exception clause in a past deed. That's typically where a severance would be documented, sometimes going back to an original homestead patent.

faqs.q: If you own the surface, do you get any royalty from drilling underneath it?
faqs.a: Not unless you also own the mineral rights. A surface-only owner has no claim to production royalty, though Utah practice generally entitles them to compensation for surface damage caused by drilling operations.

items.name: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI)
items.meta: An overriding royalty interest is carved from a lease, not the mineral estate, and expires when that lease ends. Here's how ORRIs work and what they're worth.

sections.html:
An overriding royalty interest is a different kind of asset from the mineral rights and royalty interests covered elsewhere in this guide, and the difference matters more than it might seem at first glance.

Every other interest type we cover here — mineral rights, royalty interests, NPRIs — traces back to ownership of the underlying mineral estate itself. An ORRI doesn't. It's carved out of a specific oil and gas lease, typically retained by a landman, geologist, or intermediary who helped assemble the lease, or by a working interest owner who sells part of their operating position but keeps a royalty carved from it. The ORRI holder never owned the minerals underneath the ground at all; their interest exists only because of that one lease.

That structural difference has a real consequence: an ORRI is a 'creature of the lease,' as it's often described, and it lives and dies with that lease. If the lease terminates — the primary term expires with no well drilled, or the well stops producing and the lease lapses — the ORRI terminates with it and reverts to nothing. A mineral or royalty interest tied to the underlying estate, by contrast, survives a lease expiring and simply becomes unleased minerals again. This is the single most important fact to understand if you hold, or are considering buying, an Utah ORRI.

sections.title: Where Utah ORRIs typically come from
sections.html:
In the Uinta Basin and other Utah plays, ORRIs commonly originated with landmen or small operators who assembled acreage positions, took a carved-out override as part of their compensation for putting a deal together, and later sold or passed down that override separately from the working interest itself. It's also common for a working interest owner to sell down their operating position to a larger operator while retaining an ORRI as a way to keep some upside without continuing to bear drilling and operating costs.

Because of that origin, ORRIs often show up in family portfolios connected to someone who was professionally involved in the oil and gas business at some point, rather than through inheritance of an old homestead. If you're not sure whether your interest is an ORRI or a standard royalty interest tied to mineral ownership, the conveyance document that created it, and specifically whether it references a lease or the mineral estate itself, will usually settle the question.

sections.title: How lease dependency shapes value
sections.html:
Because an ORRI's entire existence depends on one specific lease staying active, valuing it requires looking closely at where that lease actually stands: is it held by production from an existing well, meaning the lease will likely continue indefinitely as long as the well produces economically, or is it still in a primary term with drilling not yet underway, meaning there's real risk the lease — and the ORRI along with it — simply expires with nothing paid.

An ORRI on a well that's been producing steadily for years, with the lease clearly held by production, is a comparatively stable asset, similar in practice to a royalty interest, just legally distinct in its origin. An ORRI on an undrilled lease approaching the end of its primary term carries meaningfully more risk, and that risk gets reflected directly in what a buyer will offer.

sections.title: Selling an ORRI
sections.html:
We buy ORRIs across Utah, and the process starts the same way as any other interest: confirming the conveyance language, identifying the specific lease and well the override is tied to, and reviewing the production and lease status. Because the lease-dependency risk is central to ORRI value, we're especially careful here to document current lease status clearly, both for our own diligence and so you understand exactly what's driving the number.

If your ORRI is on a long-producing, held-by-production well, it can be a genuinely attractive interest to sell for a clean lump sum. If it's tied to an undrilled or expiring lease, we'll walk through that risk with you directly rather than pricing it as if it were a stable, long-lived asset.

faqs.q: What happens to your ORRI if the lease expires?
faqs.a: It terminates along with the lease. An overriding royalty interest only exists because of the specific lease it was carved from, so if that lease expires without a well drilled, or a producing well stops production and the lease lapses, the ORRI ends with it and reverts to nothing.

faqs.q: Is an ORRI the same as a royalty interest?
faqs.a: No. A royalty interest ties back to ownership of the mineral estate itself and survives a lease expiring. An ORRI is carved out of one specific lease and only exists as long as that lease does. The economics of receiving royalty payments look similar while the lease is active, but the underlying legal foundation is different.

faqs.q: How do you know if your interest is an ORRI?
faqs.a: Check the conveyance document that created it. If it references a specific oil and gas lease rather than the mineral estate, and doesn't grant any underlying mineral ownership, it's likely an ORRI. We can review the language with you if it's unclear.

faqs.q: Are ORRIs worth less than mineral rights?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on the status of the underlying lease. An ORRI on a well that's been held by production for years can be a solid, comparatively stable asset. One tied to an undrilled or soon-to-expire lease carries real risk of terminating with no value, which affects what a buyer will pay.

items.name: Working Interests
items.meta: A working interest carries drilling and operating costs alongside royalty upside. Here's how Utah working interests differ from royalty ownership, and what to weigh.

sections.html:
A working interest is the one mineral-related position that turns you into something closer to a co-operator than a passive owner, and that distinction has real financial consequences.

Everything else in this guide describes ownership positions where you receive income without bearing cost — mineral rights, royalty interests, NPRIs, and even ORRIs all sit on the cost-free side of the ledger. A working interest is different: it's the operating interest in a lease, and holding one means you're responsible for your proportionate share of drilling, completion, and ongoing operating costs, on top of being entitled to a share of revenue. In exchange for taking on that cost exposure, a working interest owner typically receives a larger percentage of production revenue than a royalty owner would on the same well.

We occasionally hear from Utah families who inherited a working interest, often from a relative who was directly involved in a small drilling venture or partnership decades ago, and are surprised to learn that the position comes with ongoing financial obligations rather than simply a bigger check. That surprise is exactly why this interest type deserves its own careful look before deciding what to do with it.

sections.title: What cost exposure actually looks like
sections.html:
A working interest owner is billed their proportionate share of expenses through what's called a joint interest billing, or JIB, covering everything from the original drilling and completion cost to ongoing operating expenses like workovers, equipment repairs, and eventually plugging and abandonment when the well reaches the end of its life. These bills arrive whether or not the well is currently profitable, and an owner who doesn't pay a cash call can face penalties under the joint operating agreement, including having their interest go non-consent on future operations or, in some structures, being subject to a lien.

This cost exposure is the core reason working interests are considered a fundamentally different risk category from royalty ownership. A royalty owner's downside in a bad month is simply a small or zero check. A working interest owner's downside can include being billed for expenses that exceed the well's revenue in a given period, particularly during a major workover or a low commodity price stretch.

sections.title: Why most family-held working interests get sold
sections.html:
For a family without operating expertise or the appetite to review and pay joint interest billings on an ongoing basis, a working interest is often more liability than asset, even when the underlying well is a solid producer. Unlike a royalty interest, it requires active management: reviewing JIBs for accuracy, responding to authorization-for-expenditure requests before major operations, and staying current on payments to avoid penalty provisions.

This is a large part of why we see more working interests sold than held once they pass to a generation not directly involved in oil and gas operations. Converting a cost-bearing operating position into a lump sum removes both the ongoing cash-call exposure and the administrative burden of tracking joint interest billings, in exchange for giving up the larger revenue share a working interest carries while it's producing well.

sections.title: How working interests get valued and sold
sections.html:
Pricing a working interest requires more diligence than a royalty interest, because a buyer needs to understand both the revenue side and the full cost picture: current operating expenses, any outstanding authorizations for expenditure, plugging liability that may eventually attach to the interest, and the terms of the underlying joint operating agreement. We review all of that before making an offer, and we're upfront that a working interest sale process typically takes a bit longer than a straightforward royalty sale because of the additional documentation involved.

If you've inherited or otherwise ended up holding a Utah working interest and aren't sure what obligations currently attach to it, that uncertainty itself is worth resolving quickly, since unpaid joint interest billings can accumulate penalties the longer they go unaddressed. We can help identify the operator and pull your current standing as a first step, whether or not you ultimately decide to sell.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a working interest and a royalty interest?
faqs.a: A royalty interest receives production revenue with no cost obligation. A working interest receives a larger revenue share but is also responsible for its proportionate share of drilling and operating costs, billed through joint interest billings.

faqs.q: Can you be billed for costs even if you don't want to pay?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if you hold the working interest and don't formally elect non-consent on a specific operation under the joint operating agreement. Unpaid joint interest billings can trigger penalty provisions, so it's worth understanding your specific agreement's terms.

faqs.q: Why would someone sell a working interest instead of keeping the higher revenue share?
faqs.a: The ongoing cost exposure and administrative burden of reviewing billings and expenditure requests often outweighs the benefit for a family without operating involvement, especially compared to the simplicity of a royalty interest. A sale converts that ongoing obligation into a clean, known amount.

faqs.q: Does a working interest carry plugging liability?
faqs.a: It can, depending on the joint operating agreement and how the interest is structured. This is one of the reasons working interest valuations require more diligence than royalty interests, and it's something we review carefully before making an offer.

items.name: Uinta Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own minerals in the Uinta Basin's Green River formation? See how waxy crude economics, SITLA checkerboard land, and county royalty history shape a sale decision.

sections.html:
Duchesne and Uintah county minerals sit inside one of the more unusual crude markets in the Lower 48, and that uniqueness cuts both ways on value.

The Uinta Basin is not a typical Rockies oil play, and any conversation about what a mineral interest there is worth has to start with that difference. The Green River formation crude produced around Altamont-Bluebell and Monument Butte is waxy: it gels at room temperature and has historically needed heated pipelines, insulated rail cars, or blending to move to refineries, most of which sit north over Indian Canyon or Soldier Summit toward the Salt Lake City market. That logistics reality has always shown up as a price differential against benchmark crude, and it is one of the first things we look at when we're pricing a Duchesne or Uintah county interest for a family that's weighing a sale.

The other defining feature of the basin is the checkerboard. Because of how the Uinta Reservation and adjoining public land were surveyed and later opened, mineral ownership in this basin alternates in ways that are unusual even by Rockies standards: a section held by the State of Utah through SITLA, a neighboring section in Ute Indian Tribe trust status, another under BLM federal minerals, and private fee minerals mixed through all of it. We treat that pattern as a fact of the basin, not a complication to be talked around, because it directly affects who your operator answers to, how a spacing unit gets pooled, and how quickly a division order clears title.

sections.title: Where the activity actually sits
sections.html:
Historically, the productive core of the basin runs through the Altamont-Bluebell field near the town of Altamont and the deeper Monument Butte / Greater Monument Butte complex south toward Myton and Roosevelt. Operators active in the basin over the past decade have included Ovintiv (through legacy Newfield Exploration acreage), Crescent Point Energy and its successor Verdun Oil, Berry Petroleum, and more recently XCL Resources and Wapiti Energy consolidating positions in the Monument Butte area. That consolidation matters for a mineral owner: when a handful of larger, better-capitalized operators absorb legacy positions, permitting and drilling tend to become more predictable, which is one of the inputs that shapes how an interest gets priced.

Position within the field matters as much as which field. Interests inside the core fairway of Altamont-Bluebell or Monument Butte, where multiple stacked Green River benches have already been developed, carry a different risk profile than flank acreage on the edges of the play where wells are thinner and less consistent. If you're not sure which side of that line your interest falls on, that's typically the first thing worth establishing before you weigh a sale against holding.

sections.title: SITLA, tribal trust minerals, and why jurisdiction changes the analysis
sections.html:
A meaningful share of Uinta Basin mineral ownership runs through the Utah School and Institutional Trust Lands Administration. SITLA sections were granted to Utah at statehood to generate revenue for public schools, and SITLA manages its own leasing program separate from private fee minerals, often with different royalty rates and different notice requirements. If your family's interest is fee minerals adjacent to or checkerboarded with SITLA sections, that neighboring state ownership can affect unit configuration and how quickly an operator can assemble a workable spacing unit.

Minerals held in trust for the Ute Indian Tribe or individual tribal allottees follow a still different track, administered through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, and those parcels do not transact the way fee minerals do. We're careful in conversations with Duchesne and Uintah county families to separate what's actually severed, privately held fee mineral estate — which is what we buy — from land that only looks similar on a plat map but sits under an entirely different ownership and leasing structure.

sections.title: What waxy crude means for the numbers
sections.html:
Because Uinta Basin crude has historically required special handling to reach market, buyers who are pricing an interest here look past the simple wellhead price and toward the netback after gathering, heating, and transport costs, as well as toward how each operator has structured its takeaway arrangements. Rail-loading capacity out of the basin and pipeline connectivity improvements have shifted that netback meaningfully over different periods, so recent royalty statements matter more here than a rule of thumb pulled from a different Rockies basin.

We'd rather build a Uinta Basin offer off your actual trailing royalty history, current activity on your specific section or unit, and the operator's recent permitting pattern than off a generic per-acre figure, because the waxy-crude differential and the checkerboard ownership pattern both move that number more than they would elsewhere. If liquidity, diversification, or simplifying an estate is the goal, we can walk through what a sale would look like against continuing to hold and collect statements as-is.

faqs.q: Why does Uinta Basin crude sell for less than other Rockies oil?
faqs.a: Green River formation crude in this basin is paraffinic, or waxy, meaning it solidifies at normal ambient temperatures and has traditionally required heated pipeline segments, insulated rail cars, or blending with lighter crude to move efficiently to market. That added handling cost has historically shown up as a price differential against benchmark crude, and it factors into how royalty income and a mineral interest's value are calculated.

faqs.q: your section is SITLA land next to your private minerals. Does that affect you?
faqs.a: It can. SITLA manages its own leasing separately from fee mineral owners, and checkerboarded SITLA sections influence how an operator assembles a spacing or drilling unit around your acreage. It's worth confirming exactly which sections are SITLA, which are BLM, and which are private fee minerals before assuming your interest behaves like a neighbor's.

faqs.q: Is your interest inside the Ute Indian Tribe trust?
faqs.a: Tribal trust and allotted minerals are administered through the Bureau of Indian Affairs and are not the same as privately held fee mineral estate, even when they sit in the same section or township. If there's any ambiguity, the county recorder's chain of title and your division order paperwork are the places to confirm status before assuming it's a fee interest that could be sold.

faqs.q: Are Monument Butte and Altamont-Bluebell still being drilled?
faqs.a: Activity has ebbed and flowed with commodity prices and operator consolidation, and it varies by section. Recent operators including XCL Resources, Wapiti Energy, and Verdun Oil have continued permitting in parts of the field. We look at current permit activity on your specific unit rather than basin-wide headlines when we're forming an offer.

faqs.q: How do you value a Duchesne or Uintah county interest?
faqs.a: We start with your recent royalty statements, the operator's permitting pattern on your unit, and where your acreage sits relative to the core of Altamont-Bluebell or Monument Butte versus the flank. Given the waxy-crude differential and checkerboard ownership here, a generic per-acre number tends to miss the mark, so we'd rather work from your actual documentation.

items.name: How to Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: A patient, portfolio-minded walkthrough of selling Utah mineral rights: valuing the interest, vetting a buyer, and closing without surprises.

sections.html:
Selling a mineral interest is a small number of decisions made in the right order, not a single transaction you either understand or don't.

Owners come to this decision from very different starting points. Some are managing an active Uinta Basin interest that's been producing for years and want to convert it to cash for a specific purpose. Others hold a small, quiet fractional share from a grandparent's estate that has paid almost nothing and they're not sure it's worth the paperwork to keep tracking. Both situations follow roughly the same process, just with different questions at the front.

This is the sequence we walk owners through, in the order it usually makes sense to think about it.

sections.title: Start with what you actually own
sections.html:
Pull your deed and figure out whether you hold minerals only, or minerals with an existing lease, or a producing royalty interest already generating checks. Each of those is a different asset to price. A leased-but-undeveloped interest carries speculative value tied to whether a well ever gets drilled; a producing royalty interest can be evaluated against real cash flow and decline trend; an unleased interest with no activity nearby is worth the least until something changes in the area.

If you're unsure which category you're in, your last royalty statement (or the absence of one) usually answers the question.

sections.title: Understand what drives the range you'll be quoted
sections.html:
Buyers price mineral interests against recent production history, nearby drilling activity, remaining decline curve, commodity price environment, and the specific play position — whether your acreage sits in the core of the Uinta oil fairway near Roosevelt and Myton, on the Paradox Basin gas trend in San Juan County, or further from current activity. We can't promise a specific number here because it genuinely depends on all of those factors and moves with them, but we can walk you through how each one affects the range for your particular interest once we see your documents.

Be wary of anyone quoting a firm number before reviewing your deed and recent statements. A credible range comes from your actual production and title history, not a generic per-acre figure pulled from a website.

sections.title: Get more than one perspective before you commit
sections.html:
Even if you intend to sell to us, it's reasonable to get a second read on your interest, particularly if it's a larger or actively producing asset. A second offer, or a conversation with a landman or attorney familiar with Utah mineral title, gives you a sanity check on the range you've been quoted. We'd rather you feel confident in the decision than rush it.

For smaller, quiet interests that have never produced, this step matters less — the diligence cost of shopping a tiny fractional share around often outweighs any difference in price you'd find.

sections.title: Closing: what actually happens
sections.html:
Once you accept an offer, the buyer prepares a mineral deed transferring your interest, along with closing documents confirming your identity and, if relevant, your standing as heir or successor. Funds typically move by wire or check once the signed, notarized deed is received and recorded with the county. From accepted offer to funded closing is usually a matter of weeks, not months, assuming title is straightforward — longer if there's an heirship or boundary question to resolve first.

If your acreage sits near a SITLA state trust section or on federal split estate, expect the title review to take a bit longer while the buyer confirms your legal description doesn't overlap that boundary. This is routine on Utah checkerboard land and shouldn't derail a sale, just extend the timeline modestly.

faqs.q: How long does it take to sell mineral rights in Utah?
faqs.a: A straightforward sale with clean title can close in a few weeks. Interests with unresolved heirship, multiple owners, or a title question against a state trust boundary take longer while that's sorted out.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell your whole interest?
faqs.a: No. Many owners sell a portion of their mineral or royalty interest and keep the rest, which lets you take some liquidity now while retaining upside if activity increases later.

faqs.q: What if your interest has never produced anything?
faqs.a: It can still have value, particularly if it sits near active drilling or a play that's expanding. The range will simply reflect that it's currently speculative rather than cash-flowing.

faqs.q: Will you owe taxes on the sale?
faqs.a: Likely, in the form of capital gains treatment on the sale proceeds, though the specifics depend on your basis and holding period. Talk to your CPA or tax advisor about your particular situation before closing.

faqs.q: What if several family members inherited the interest together?
faqs.a: Each heir generally needs to be identified on the deed and closing paperwork, and each typically signs for their own fractional share. It helps to coordinate among family members early so the process isn't held up waiting on one signature at the end.

faqs.q: Can you sell an interest that still has an active lease on it?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer purchases the mineral or royalty interest subject to the existing lease, meaning the lease terms carry forward and the buyer steps into your position as lessor going forward.

items.name: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
items.meta: What actually drives Utah mineral rights value — production, decline, play position, and SITLA or split-estate boundary factors — explained plainly.

sections.html:
Every owner asks the same first question, and the honest answer is always: it depends on a handful of specific things about your particular interest.

We understand why a straight number feels like the useful answer. It isn't, and any buyer who gives you one before seeing your deed and recent production history is either guessing or lowballing. What we can do is walk through the actual factors that move value up or down for interests like yours, so you can judge any offer you receive against something real rather than a headline figure.

This guide covers producing and non-producing interests separately, since they're valued through different lenses, and closes with the Utah-specific wrinkles worth knowing about.

sections.title: If your interest is already producing
sections.html:
Value tracks closely with your trailing production, the well's decline trend, and the current price environment for oil or gas. A royalty interest generating steady checks off a well several years into a long, shallow decline tail is a more predictable asset than one still on the steep early decline of a new horizontal well, even if the newer well is currently paying more per month. Buyers project the remaining income forward and discount it to a present value, weighting for how confident that projection can be.

Nearby drilling matters too. An interest in a unit where the operator is actively developing offset wells carries more near-term upside than one sitting quietly with no announced activity, and that gets reflected in any range you're quoted.

sections.title: If your interest has never produced
sections.html:
Undeveloped or unleased minerals are valued more speculatively, based mainly on proximity to current drilling and the general trajectory of the play. Acreage in the core of the Uinta oil fairway, where operators have a long track record with waxy crude wells around Duchesne and Uintah counties, generally holds more speculative value than acreage on the quieter margins of the Paradox Basin gas trend, where drilling has been intermittent for years.

This kind of interest is harder to price with precision, and any range offered on it should be understood as reflecting probability of future development, not a guarantee of it.

sections.title: Utah-specific factors worth knowing
sections.html:
Checkerboard ownership is the defining feature of mineral title in this state. Sections of SITLA-managed state trust land are interleaved with federal, tribal, and private minerals across much of the Uinta Basin, a legacy of the original federal land grant to Utah at statehood. Acreage near an actively leased SITLA section can be a useful signal of operator interest in the area, since the state trust land office manages its leasing on a fairly transparent, market-driven basis.

Split estate — where surface ownership was severed from mineral ownership generations ago, often through original homestead patents — is also common here and affects how straightforward surface access for drilling has historically been in a given township, which buyers weigh alongside the geology itself.

sections.title: What actually moves the number
sections.html: In rough order of impact: recent production trend, remaining decline curve if producing, proximity to active drilling if not, current commodity price levels, and title clarity, including whether heirship or a checkerboard boundary needs resolving before closing. A clean, well-documented interest with recent statements in hand will generally see a faster, more confident offer than one requiring title work first — not necessarily a different final value, but a smoother path to it.

faqs.q: Why won't you just give you a price per acre?
faqs.a: Because value here depends heavily on production history, decline trend, and nearby activity, all of which vary enormously even within the same county. A generic per-acre figure would mislead more than it would help — we'd rather review your actual interest first.

faqs.q: Does owning minerals near a SITLA state trust section help your value?
faqs.a: It can be a useful signal of operator interest in the area, since state trust land leasing tends to be active and market-driven, but it's one factor among several, not a guarantee of higher value on its own.

faqs.q: How much does the current price of oil affect what your interest is worth?
faqs.a: Meaningfully, particularly for producing interests, since value is built on a forward price assumption. A higher price environment generally supports higher valuations, and a lower one the reverse.

faqs.q: your interest has never produced anything — is it worth anything at all?
faqs.a: Often yes, especially if it sits near active drilling, though the value reflects probability of future development rather than current cash flow. We can walk through what nearby activity looks like for your specific township.

faqs.q: If you have several small fractional interests inherited from different relatives, Should you value them together or separately?
faqs.a: Separately, at least initially, since each may trace back to a different tract with its own production history and title status. Once each is understood individually, it's reasonable to bundle them into a single sale conversation for convenience.

faqs.q: Does the size of your interest, large or small, change how it's valued?
faqs.a: The underlying method stays the same, but very small fractional interests sometimes carry less buyer interest simply due to the administrative cost of closing relative to the payment size, which is worth keeping in mind when weighing whether to sell.

items.name: Reading Your Royalty Statements
items.meta: A plain-language walkthrough of the Utah royalty statement: deductions, price codes, decline curves, and what to flag before you decide whether to hold or sell.

sections.html:
Most owners we talk with in the Uinta and Paradox basins have a drawer full of royalty stubs they have never really read line by line.

A royalty statement is the one document that tells the truth about what an interest is actually producing, month over month, after the operator's deductions are taken. Families who inherited a fractional interest from a grandparent's allotment often treat the check as the whole story. It isn't. The statement behind the check carries the volume, the price, the deduction code, and the well or unit name — the pieces that let you (or an advisor working for you) judge whether an interest is worth holding, worth leasing again, or worth selling now while activity is visible.

We read statements as part of every conversation with an owner, and we walk through this same breakdown before we ever quote a range. The goal here is to give you the same literacy, whether you sell to us, to someone else, or not at all this year.

sections.title: The line items that actually matter
sections.html:
Ignore the logo at the top and go straight to five columns: property or well name, production month, gross volume, price per barrel or mcf, and net decimal interest. The net decimal is your ownership fraction after unitization — it is usually a long string like 0.00041237 and it rarely matches the fraction you think you own, because spacing units, pooling, and prior severances all touch it.

Below that sits the deduction section, sometimes labeled 'post-production costs' or 'gathering, processing, transportation.' In the Uinta Basin, where waxy crude has to be heated and trucked or railed to a Salt Lake refinery before it can be sold, these deductions run higher than in basins with pipeline takeaway. That is not a red flag by itself — it is the cost structure of the play — but it is the number you want to track statement over statement to see if it is creeping.

sections.title: Price codes and why your barrel isn't WTI
sections.html:
Uinta black wax and yellow wax crude sell at a differential to benchmark prices because of the heating, trucking, and refining logistics unique to this basin. A statement showing $8 or more under WTI on a given month is normal for this geology, not a sign you are being shorted. What you want to watch is whether that differential is widening over time relative to nearby wells, which can signal a change in takeaway capacity or refinery demand rather than anything about your specific interest.

For gas interests tied to Paradox Basin or older Uinta Basin gas wells, the same logic applies against a regional gas hub price rather than Henry Hub. Ask for the index name on the statement if it isn't printed plainly — most operators will provide it if you call the owner relations line.

sections.title: Decline, and what a falling check actually tells you
sections.html:
Oil and gas wells decline. A statement that shows volume falling 20 to 40 percent in year two versus year one off a new horizontal well is typical decline curve behavior, not a problem with your interest. What matters is the shape of the decline after that first steep drop — a well that stabilizes into a long, shallow tail can still support meaningful royalty income for a decade or more, while one that keeps falling sharply may be nearing its economic limit.

This is exactly where a portfolio decision comes in. An interest riding a steep decline curve is worth less to a buyer with each passing quarter, because the buyer is pricing a shrinking future income stream. If you are weighing whether to sell, the trend across your last six to twelve statements tells you more than any single month's check.

sections.title: Suspense, non-consent, and other flags worth a phone call
sections.html: Some statements show a line for funds held 'in suspense' — often because of an unresolved title issue, a missing heirship affidavit, or a division order that was never returned. On split-estate and checkerboard state trust land parcels common across the Uinta Basin, where SITLA-managed sections sit interleaved with federal and private minerals, title clean-up can take longer than owners expect, and suspended funds can sit for years until it's resolved. It is worth calling the operator's owner relations department once a year just to ask if anything is being held for your interest.

faqs.q: Why does your net decimal interest look so small?
faqs.a: Spacing and pooling divide production across every mineral owner in the unit rather than only the acreage directly under the wellbore, so a fractional inherited interest translates into a long decimal. It's normal and doesn't mean your interest is wrong — ask the operator for the unit's pooling order if you want to verify the math.

faqs.q: your statement shows a lower price than what you see quoted in the news. Is that a mistake?
faqs.a: Usually not. Uinta waxy crude sells at a real, persistent differential to WTI because of the heating and trucking required to move it, and gas often prices off a regional index rather than Henry Hub. Compare your price against prior months on the same statement rather than against a national headline number.

faqs.q: What does a 'suspense' line mean and Should you worry?
faqs.a: It means the operator is holding funds tied to your interest, usually pending a title or heirship document. It is common on older, inherited interests and on parcels with a mixed state-trust and federal history. Call the owner relations line and ask what document is needed to release it.

faqs.q: Can you use your royalty statements when you is deciding whether to sell?
faqs.a: Yes, and you should. Six to twelve months of statements show volume trend, price trend, and deduction trend, which is exactly what a buyer prices when quoting a range. Bring recent statements to any conversation about selling, whether it's with us or another party.

items.name: Division Orders Explained
items.meta: A family-office style breakdown of the division order — what it verifies, why it can stall payment on Uinta Basin checkerboard parcels, and when to sign.

sections.html:
The division order is the one document that turns a title opinion into an actual check, and on Utah's checkerboard mineral ownership it deserves more attention than most owners give it.

A division order is the operator's written confirmation of your decimal share in a well or unit, sent so you can verify the math before the first payment goes out. It is not a lease and it does not transfer ownership of anything. Treat it as a receipt you are being asked to check, not a contract you are being asked to accept blind.

We see two very different reactions to this document. Some owners sign whatever arrives without reading it, and others let it sit in a drawer for years out of confusion, which quietly stops payment. Neither is the right approach on interests where the underlying title runs through a mix of federal allotment, private fee minerals, and Utah's SITLA-managed state trust sections.

sections.title: What the document is actually confirming
sections.html:
At its core, the division order restates your net revenue interest — the fraction of production revenue you are entitled to after royalty burdens, overrides, and any prior conveyances are netted out. That fraction should trace back to your deed, your probate or heirship documents, and the pooling or unitization order for the specific well. If any of those source documents changed hands recently, through a sale, a gift, or an inheritance, the division order needs to reflect the new owner before checks will move.

Operators build these decimals from a title opinion, and title opinions on Uinta Basin acreage are frequently complicated by checkerboard ownership, where a single spacing unit can straddle a SITLA state trust parcel, a federal split-estate tract, and privately held minerals in adjoining sections. That mix is exactly why division orders here can take longer to issue than in a basin with cleaner, single-source title.

sections.title: Why signing late — or not at all — costs you
sections.html:
Unsigned division orders are one of the most common reasons royalty funds sit in suspense. Most operators will hold payment, sometimes for years, until the decimal is confirmed in writing, even though the well is producing and revenue is accruing on your behalf. That money isn't lost, but it also isn't earning anything for you while it waits, and if you are weighing an offer on the interest, a buyer will discount for the uncertainty a stalled division order represents.

The fix is usually simple: read the decimal against your own records, call the owner relations desk with any discrepancy, and return the signed order. If the decimal looks wrong, say so in writing before signing — a phone call alone rarely creates a record the operator will act on.

sections.title: Where the checkerboard adds friction
sections.html:
State trust land administered by SITLA generates royalty income that flows back to Utah's school and institutional trust beneficiaries, and SITLA's own leasing and division-order handling runs on a separate track from private mineral owners in the same unit. If your interest sits adjacent to or intermingled with a SITLA section, expect the operator's landman to take extra time reconciling the boundary, especially on older sections where the original federal patent, state selection, and private conveyance chain haven't been fully cross-referenced.

This is not a reason to worry about your interest — it is a reason to expect the paperwork to move on a slower calendar than a straightforward fee-mineral tract elsewhere in the country, and to keep your own deed and probate records organized so you can answer questions quickly when the landman calls.

faqs.q: Does signing a division order affect your ownership of the minerals?
faqs.a: No. It only confirms your share of revenue from a specific well or unit for payment purposes. Ownership of the underlying minerals is established by your deed and heirship, not by the division order.

faqs.q: What if the decimal on your division order looks too small?
faqs.a: Compare it against your deed and any prior statements. Common causes are pooling across a larger spacing unit than you expected, or a prior partial conveyance you may not be aware of. Call the operator's owner relations line and put your question in writing.

faqs.q: Why is your division order taking so long on a Uinta Basin well?
faqs.a: Checkerboard title involving SITLA state trust sections, federal split estate, and private minerals in the same unit takes longer to reconcile than clean fee-mineral title. It's common in this basin and usually not a sign of a problem with your specific interest.

faqs.q: Should you sign a division order before selling your interest?
faqs.a: It helps. A confirmed decimal and a payment history give a buyer a cleaner picture of the interest and can support a faster, better-informed offer than an unresolved title situation would.

faqs.q: What if you never received a division order but you know a well was drilled near your acreage?
faqs.a: Contact the operator directly and ask whether your tract falls within the unit. Sometimes an owner is simply missed if a prior address on file is out of date, especially on interests that changed hands through inheritance without the operator being notified of the new owner.

faqs.q: Can more than one operator send you a division order for the same acreage?
faqs.a: Yes, if different wells or units cover overlapping or adjoining portions of your interest, particularly common on checkerboard acreage where multiple spacing units can touch the same section. Each division order should be reviewed on its own for the specific decimal it covers.

items.name: Documents You Need to Sell
items.meta: The documents an Uinta or Paradox Basin mineral owner should gather before requesting an offer, and why title clean-up matters more here than elsewhere.

sections.html:
The single fastest way to move from first phone call to closed transaction is having your paperwork organized before anyone asks for it.

We spend a good portion of every early conversation helping owners figure out what they actually hold, because Utah mineral title has a way of accumulating layers over a few generations — a deed here, a probate there, a name that changed at marriage, a section that turned out to sit against a SITLA state trust boundary nobody mentioned. None of that is unusual, and none of it should scare you off. It just means the paperwork stage benefits from a little preparation.

Below is the working list we use ourselves. You do not need every item to start a conversation, but having what you can find in one folder will shorten the time between an offer and a closed transaction considerably.

sections.title: The deed chain
sections.html:
Start with the deed that shows how the minerals came to you or your family — a warranty deed, a mineral deed, or a quitclaim. If you inherited the interest, the deed may be decades old and reference a grantor you never met. That's fine; it's still the anchor document. If you don't have a copy, the county recorder's office in the county where the minerals sit (Duchesne, Uintah, Grand, or San Juan, depending on where your acreage falls) can usually pull a certified copy for a small fee.

If the interest passed through more than one generation, gather every deed in the chain you can find rather than only the most recent one. Gaps in the chain are common and are usually fixable, but they take time to trace, so surfacing them early keeps a sale on schedule.

sections.title: Probate and heirship records
sections.html:
If you received the interest through inheritance rather than a direct conveyance, you'll need whatever probate order, affidavit of heirship, or small estate affidavit established your ownership. Utah probate on mineral interests can sometimes be handled through a simplified process if the estate was small and uncontested, but if the original owner passed without a will, or if there are multiple heirs who never formally divided the interest, that needs to be resolved — or at least clearly documented — before a sale can close cleanly.

Multiple-heir situations are extremely common on interests that trace back to original homestead or allotment land in the Uinta Basin. If you're one of several siblings or cousins who each hold a fraction, it helps to know who else is on the deed before you start.

sections.title: Recent royalty statements and any lease
sections.html:
Bring the last six to twelve months of royalty statements if the interest is currently producing, along with a copy of any active oil and gas lease. The statements show real volume and price history, which grounds any conversation about value in fact rather than guesswork. The lease tells a buyer what royalty rate, primary term, and any special provisions apply, which matters directly to what the interest is worth to acquire.

If the interest has never produced, or the lease expired years ago, that's useful information too — say so plainly rather than leaving it out, since it changes how the interest should be evaluated.

sections.title: A note on state trust and split-estate parcels
sections.html: If your acreage borders or overlaps a SITLA state trust section, or sits on federal split estate where the surface and minerals were severed at different times, mention it up front. It doesn't disqualify a sale, but a buyer will want to understand the boundary and any prior state leasing history on the adjoining section before finalizing a number, and having that context early avoids a delay later in the process.

faqs.q: What if you can't find your original deed?
faqs.a: The county recorder's office where the minerals are located can typically provide a certified copy for a small fee. Tell us the county and we can point you toward the right office.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: Not always, but if your title involves multiple heirs, an unresolved probate, or a boundary question against state trust land, an attorney can save time. We're happy to work alongside whoever you choose to consult.

faqs.q: What if you only own a small fractional interest?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests, often from an original family allotment split among many heirs over generations, are common in this basin. Bring whatever documentation you have and we'll help identify what's still needed.

faqs.q: Is there a deadline to gather all this before you can get an offer?
faqs.a: No. We can give you a preliminary range based on limited information and refine it as documents come in. A complete file just moves the closing process faster once you decide to proceed.

faqs.q: What if your name on the deed doesn't match your current legal name?
faqs.a: Common after marriage, divorce, or a legal name change. Bring documentation of the name change, such as a marriage certificate or court order, so the closing paperwork can tie your current identity back to the deed on record.

items.name: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
items.meta: Warning signs of an undervalued Utah mineral rights offer, and the questions worth asking before signing anything a buyer sends you.

sections.html:
Mineral owners in this basin get mailers and cold calls constantly, and the quality of those offers varies far more than most people expect.

We're a buyer, and we know that puts us in an odd position to write this. We think it's worth writing anyway, because an owner who understands what a fair process looks like makes a better decision whether they sell to us or to someone else. A rushed or pressured sale rarely serves the owner's interest, and the warning signs are usually visible if you know what to look for.

None of this is about assuming bad faith from every buyer. Plenty of legitimate companies operate in this space. It's about knowing the difference between a firm grounded in your actual production history and one working off a template.

sections.title: A firm number before they've seen your deed
sections.html:
If a buyer quotes you an exact dollar figure, or a firm per-acre price, before reviewing your deed, your county, and your recent production, treat that as a sales tactic rather than a valuation. Value here depends on decline trend, nearby drilling, and title clarity — none of which can be assessed from a mailer that only knows your name and county from public tax records. A credible offer follows a request for your documents, not the other way around.

It's reasonable to ask directly: what specifically did you review to arrive at this number? A buyer who can answer with your production data or nearby comparable activity is working in good faith. One who can't is guessing, likely low.

sections.title: Artificial urgency
sections.html: Offers with a short fuse — sign within a week or the number drops — are a pressure tactic, not a reflection of any real market timing constraint on a mineral title transaction. Legitimate buyers understand that owners need time to review paperwork, ask questions, and in some cases get a second opinion. There is essentially never a legitimate reason a mineral rights offer needs to expire in 48 hours.

sections.title: Vague or missing deed language
sections.html:
Read whatever purchase agreement or deed you're sent carefully, or have someone read it for you. Watch for language conveying more than you intended — for example, a deed that sweeps in executive rights, future lease bonuses, or an unusually broad legal description beyond the specific tract you meant to sell. On checkerboard acreage near a SITLA state trust boundary, an imprecise legal description is a real risk worth catching before you sign, not after.

A trustworthy buyer will walk you through the deed language before asking for a signature and won't push back on you taking it to an attorney first.

sections.title: No verifiable track record or contact information
sections.html: A legitimate buyer should be reachable by phone, willing to answer questions about how they arrived at their number, and comfortable with you taking time to think it over or compare it against another offer. If a company is difficult to reach once you've expressed interest, or dodges specific questions about your interest, that's worth noticing before you sign anything.

sections.title: A price that ignores your basin entirely
sections.html: Be cautious of a buyer whose reasoning could apply to acreage anywhere in the country — no mention of waxy crude differentials, decline behavior specific to your well, or the checkerboard title common to this state. A firm that hasn't taken the time to say anything specific about Utah, the Uinta Basin, or your county likely hasn't taken the time to look closely at your interest either, and the number that follows tends to reflect that.

faqs.q: Is it normal to get more than one offer on the same mineral interest?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's a reasonable thing to pursue, particularly on a larger or producing interest. Comparing offers is one of the best ways to sanity-check the range you've been given.

faqs.q: Should you be suspicious of every unsolicited mineral rights offer?
faqs.a: Not automatically, but treat a firm price arriving before any document review as a starting point for questions, not a number to accept at face value.

faqs.q: What Should you ask a buyer before agreeing to anything?
faqs.a: Ask what they reviewed to reach their number, whether the price is firm or preliminary, what the deed conveys exactly, and whether you have time to review the paperwork with someone else first. A credible buyer will answer all of these plainly.

faqs.q: Is a lower initial offer always a sign of bad faith?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Offers can vary based on how conservative a buyer's price deck or discount rate is. The distinction is whether the buyer explains their reasoning and is open to your questions, not simply whether the first number is the highest one you'll see.

faqs.q: What if a buyer refuses to put their offer in writing?
faqs.a: Treat that as a serious warning sign. A legitimate offer should be documented clearly enough that you can review it on your own time, share it with an advisor, or compare it against another buyer without relying on memory of a phone call.

items.name: Mineral Deeds & Title Transfer
items.meta: How a mineral deed transfer actually closes in Utah, from drafting through county recording, and what can slow it down on checkerboard title.

sections.html:
The deed is the quiet, unglamorous document that does all the actual legal work in a mineral rights sale, and it deserves a closer look than most owners give it.

Everything that leads up to a mineral sale — the conversation, the offer, the agreed price — is really just negotiation toward one moment: a signed, notarized mineral deed being recorded in the county where the minerals sit. Understanding what that document does, and what can slow its path to the recorder's office, takes the mystery out of the closing process.

This is written for owners who've never transferred real property before, since most people haven't, and mineral deeds carry a few wrinkles that ordinary house closings don't.

sections.title: What a mineral deed actually conveys
sections.html:
A mineral deed transfers your ownership interest in the oil, gas, and associated minerals under a described tract, separate from any surface rights, which you retain unless the deed says otherwise. The legal description matters enormously — it typically references the section, township, and range under Utah's Public Land Survey grid, along with the county. Any error in that description, even a transposed number, can cause real problems tracing title later, so it's worth reading carefully before signing rather than trusting it was typed correctly.

The deed will also state whether you're conveying all of your interest or a fractional portion, and whether it includes any executive rights (the right to negotiate future leases) or is limited to a non-participating royalty interest. Know which one you're signing before you sign it.

sections.title: Notarization and recording
sections.html:
Utah, like every state, requires the deed to be signed in front of a notary public before it can be recorded. If you live out of state, this is usually handled through a local notary near you and the signed original mailed back, or in some cases through remote online notarization where available. Once notarized, the deed is recorded with the county recorder — Duchesne, Uintah, Grand, San Juan, or wherever the minerals are located — which puts the transfer on the public record and establishes your buyer's priority against later claims.

Recording is what actually protects the buyer's interest, so a legitimate buyer will move to record promptly after closing rather than sitting on a signed deed.

sections.title: Where checkerboard title slows things down
sections.html:
If your interest sits within or adjacent to a SITLA state trust section, or on federal split estate where mineral and surface ownership diverged decades ago, the title company or attorney handling closing may take extra time confirming the legal description doesn't overlap a state or federal boundary incorrectly. This is a title-clarity step, not a sign anything is wrong with your ownership — it's simply more common in Utah's checkerboard land pattern than in states with cleaner, contiguous private mineral tracts.

Multiple-heir interests add a similar wrinkle: if you inherited alongside siblings or cousins, each heir generally needs to sign their own deed for their own fractional share, or a single deed needs every heir's signature, notarized individually if they live in different places.

sections.title: What we do to keep the process on track
sections.html: We draft the legal description directly against the county's official plat and cross-check it against your deed before anything goes out for signature, which is the step most likely to catch a boundary problem before it becomes a delay. We also confirm upfront whether any co-heirs need to sign alongside you, so the closing package is assembled once, correctly, rather than sent back and forth over missing signatures.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to sign a mineral deed?
faqs.a: Not necessarily for a straightforward transfer, but it's reasonable to have an attorney review the legal description and deed language before you sign, particularly on a larger or multi-heir interest.

faqs.q: What if you live out of state — Can you still complete the transfer?
faqs.a: Yes. This is common. The deed is typically mailed to you, signed in front of a local notary, and returned. Some closings can use remote online notarization depending on your state's rules.

faqs.q: Who pays the recording fee?
faqs.a: This is negotiated as part of the sale terms, but the buyer commonly covers recording costs as part of closing. Confirm this in writing before signing.

faqs.q: How long after signing does the deed actually record?
faqs.a: Usually within days to a couple of weeks, depending on the county recorder's processing time. Recording is what finalizes the transfer on public record.

faqs.q: What if the legal description in an old deed is unclear or hard to read?
faqs.a: This happens on older deeds tied back to original allotment or homestead patents. A title company or attorney can typically reconstruct the correct legal description from the county's plat records, though it may take a bit longer than a straightforward, clearly typed modern deed.

faqs.q: Is a mineral deed different from a regular warranty deed used for a house?
faqs.a: It's structured similarly but conveys only the mineral estate rather than surface property, and typically carries a more detailed legal description tied to the section, township, and range rather than a street address.

items.name: Lease vs. Sell: Which Is Right?
items.meta: Weighing a new lease offer against a sale on Utah mineral rights, with the tradeoffs that matter for Uinta and Paradox Basin owners specifically.

sections.html:
A landman calling with a new lease and a buyer calling with a cash offer are solving two different problems, and it helps to know which one you're actually trying to solve.

Leasing and selling are not competing versions of the same transaction. Leasing keeps you as the mineral owner and grants an operator the right to drill for a defined term in exchange for a bonus payment now and a royalty later, if and when a well is drilled and produces. Selling converts your entire future interest, whatever it turns out to be worth, into a single payment today. Neither is universally right — the better fit depends on your time horizon, your appetite for uncertainty, and what else is going on in your life around the decision.

We treat this as a portfolio question, not a sales pitch. Plenty of owners we talk with should lease, or hold, rather than sell, and we'll tell you that plainly if it looks that way.

sections.title: What leasing actually gives you
sections.html:
A lease bonus is typically a modest upfront payment per net mineral acre, paid regardless of whether a well is ever drilled. If drilling does happen and the well produces, you then earn a royalty — commonly in the twelve-to-twenty percent range depending on the lease terms negotiated — for as long as the well produces economically. The upside of leasing is that you keep ownership and participate in whatever the well actually does over its life, including any future development in the unit.

The downside is uncertainty and patience. Many leased tracts in Utah, particularly in slower parts of the Paradox Basin or on the margins of the Uinta play, never get drilled during the primary lease term and the lease simply expires, leaving you with only the original bonus. Even where drilling happens, first royalty checks can be a year or more out from signing.

sections.title: What selling actually gives you
sections.html:
A sale converts the interest — leased or unleased, producing or not — into one payment now, sized against current activity, decline trend if it's producing, and the likelihood of future development if it isn't. You give up all future upside, including any new wells drilled in the unit years from now, in exchange for certainty and immediate liquidity. For owners consolidating an estate, funding a near-term need, or simply tired of tracking small, irregular royalty checks from a fractional interest, that certainty is often worth more than the theoretical upside.

For owners sitting on a strongly performing, actively producing Uinta Basin interest with visible nearby drilling, selling the whole thing may mean walking away from real future cash flow — which is exactly why we'll often suggest selling only a portion, keeping the rest to participate in what happens next.

sections.title: Questions that tend to clarify the decision
sections.html: How many other owners hold interests in the same unit, and are they leasing or selling? Is there active drilling within a mile or two of your acreage, or is the nearest well several sections away? Do you have a near-term use for cash that outweighs the value of waiting? Is the interest large enough that a partial sale makes sense, or small enough that the administrative burden of managing it outweighs the royalty it generates? Answering these honestly usually points toward one path or the other.

faqs.q: Can you lease and still sell later?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's a common sequence. A signed lease with an established royalty rate can actually make the interest easier to value and sell later, since it removes some of the uncertainty a buyer would otherwise have to price in.

faqs.q: What happens if your lease expires without a well being drilled?
faqs.a: You keep the original bonus payment and the minerals revert to unleased status, free to lease again or sell as you choose. This is a common outcome in slower-moving parts of the Paradox Basin.

faqs.q: Is a partial sale possible if you want some cash now but don't want to give up everything?
faqs.a: Yes. Many owners sell a portion of their interest, often half, and retain the remainder to keep exposure to future drilling and royalty income.

faqs.q: Which option is better if your interest has never produced?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on nearby activity. If drilling is picking up nearby, leasing may capture more value over time; if the area has been quiet for years, a sale may be the more practical way to realize any value now rather than waiting indefinitely.

faqs.q: Does it matter if your acreage touches a SITLA state trust section?
faqs.a: It can. SITLA's own leasing activity on the adjoining section is often a useful, publicly visible signal of operator interest in the area, which can inform whether leasing your own minerals soon looks likely to attract a serious bonus offer.

faqs.q: Can you compare a lease bonus offer against a sale offer directly?
faqs.a: Not as a straight dollar comparison, since a lease bonus is only the first of potentially many payments while a sale is a single final number, but we're glad to walk through both so you can weigh them against your own priorities.

items.name: Taxes When You Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: How the sale of Utah mineral rights is typically taxed, basis and holding period basics, and why a CPA conversation belongs early in the process.

sections.html:
The tax question comes up in nearly every conversation we have, usually right after the value question, and it deserves a straight answer even though we're not the ones who can give you a final one.

We are a mineral buyer, not a CPA or tax attorney, and nothing here is tax advice for your specific situation. What we can offer is the general framework that applies to most mineral rights sales, so you walk into a conversation with your own tax advisor already understanding the shape of the question, rather than starting from zero.

The two things that matter most to how a sale is taxed are your basis in the interest and how long you've held it — both of which look different depending on whether you bought the minerals, were gifted them, or inherited them.

sections.title: Capital gains, in general terms
sections.html:
Selling a mineral interest is typically treated as a sale of a capital asset, meaning any gain above your basis is generally subject to capital gains tax rather than ordinary income tax. Whether that gain is taxed at long-term or short-term rates depends on how long you've held the interest — over a year usually qualifies for the more favorable long-term rate, though your CPA should confirm this against your specific facts, especially around inherited interests.

Basis is the number that determines the size of the taxable gain, and it's where inherited interests differ meaningfully from purchased ones.

sections.title: Basis on inherited minerals
sections.html:
If you inherited your mineral interest, your basis is generally the fair market value of the minerals at the date of the original owner's death, not what that person originally paid or what the interest was worth decades earlier. This is often called a stepped-up basis, and it can significantly reduce your taxable gain compared to what you might expect, particularly on an interest that's been in a family for a long time.

The practical challenge is documenting that date-of-death value, especially for interests that were quiet or barely producing at the time. A CPA experienced with mineral estates can often help reconstruct a reasonable valuation using historical production and pricing data if a formal appraisal wasn't done at the time.

sections.title: Basis on purchased or gifted minerals
sections.html: If you or a prior owner in your chain purchased the minerals, your basis is generally what was paid, adjusted for any depletion previously claimed on royalty income over the years. If the interest was gifted to you during the giver's lifetime rather than inherited at death, your basis is typically carried over from the giver's original basis rather than stepped up — a materially different outcome from inheritance, and one worth flagging to your CPA specifically.

sections.title: Timing and 1031 considerations
sections.html:
Some owners selling a producing mineral interest explore a 1031 exchange into replacement real property to defer the gain, since mineral interests can in some circumstances qualify as like-kind real property under current rules.
